title: Linux kernel networking and socket concurrency
description: epoll edge vs level triggering, TCP TIME_WAIT states, SYN queues, SO_REUSEPORT, and socket concurrency.

questions.text: What is the difference between Edge-Triggered (EPOLLET) and Level-Triggered (default) modes in Linux epoll?

options.text: Level-Triggered notifies as long as data remains in the buffer; Edge-Triggered notifies only when a state transition occurs (new data arrives), requiring reads until EAGAIN/EWOULDBLOCK
Level-Triggered only works with UDP sockets; Edge-Triggered only works with TCP
Edge-Triggered requires root privileges in Linux
Level-Triggered is asynchronous; Edge-Triggered is synchronous

questions.explanation: In level-triggered mode, epoll_wait returns the file descriptor every loop as long as the buffer has unread bytes. In edge-triggered mode (EPOLLET), it notifies only when new data transitions the socket, so the application must loop read() until it receives EAGAIN to avoid hanging.

questions.text: Why does a TCP connection enter the TIME_WAIT state (typically 60 seconds) after the active closer sends the final ACK?

options.text: To allow delayed duplicate packets from the old connection to expire in the network and ensure the remote host received the final ACK
To flush disk buffers to physical storage
To wait for the operating system to garbage collect open file handles
To negotiate TLS session tickets for the next connection

questions.explanation: TIME_WAIT ensures: (1) if the final ACK was lost, the peer's retransmitted FIN can be answered with another ACK; and (2) any delayed wandering duplicate segments from this connection expire (2 * MSL) so they cannot corrupt a future connection reusing the same 4-tuple (source IP, source port, dest IP, dest port).

questions.text: What socket option allows multiple independent worker processes on a multi-core server to bind to the exact same IP and port simultaneously, with the Linux kernel load-balancing incoming SYN packets across them?
questions.explanation: SO_REUSEPORT (introduced in Linux 3.9) allows multiple listening sockets to bind to the same port. The kernel evenly distributes incoming connections across worker processes using an internal 4-tuple hash, eliminating the 'thundering herd' wake-up problem on a single accept queue.

questions.text: How do TCP SYN Cookies protect a server from connection exhaustion during a SYN Flood DDoS attack?

options.text: By rejecting all incoming connection requests until the flood ceases
By encoding connection state into the initial TCP Sequence Number (ISN) sent in the SYN-ACK, avoiding allocating a half-open socket struct in the SYN backlog until the client ACK returns
By caching client IP addresses in a Redis cluster
By automatically terminating idle HTTP keep-alive connections

questions.explanation: When the SYN backlog table fills up under attack, SYN cookies compute a cryptographic hash of the 4-tuple and timestamp as the server's Initial Sequence Number (ISN). No memory is allocated. When the legitimate client sends ACK (acknowledging ISN + 1), the server decodes the cookie and creates the full socket connection.

questions.text: Setting TCP_NODELAY on a socket disables Nagle's algorithm, causing small packets to be sent immediately instead of being buffered until a full MSS or ACK arrives.
questions.explanation: True. Nagle's algorithm buffers small outbound payloads to reduce packet header overhead. Disabling it with TCP_NODELAY is essential for interactive low-latency protocols like SSH, WebSockets, and gaming, eliminating the 40-200ms delayed ACK interaction penalty.
